value.overview: The Golden-hooded Tanager is a small, brilliantly colored tropical songbird found from southern Mexico through Central America to western Colombia and Ecuador. Its golden head, black facial mask, turquoise-blue markings, and contrasting pale belly make adults highly distinctive. It inhabits humid lowland and foothill landscapes, including forest edges, secondary growth, plantations, and wooded gardens. Usually seen in pairs or small groups, it feeds mainly on fruit and insects in trees and shrubs.
value.classification: The Golden-hooded Tanager belongs to the order Passeriformes and the tanager family Thraupidae. Its scientific name is Stilpnia larvata; older references may list it as Tangara larvata.
value.identification: Adults are about 13 cm long and have a bright golden-yellow hood crossed by a broad black mask, with violet-blue or turquoise borders around the face. The back is mainly black, while the shoulders, rump, wing edges, tail edges, and flanks show vivid blue-green tones. The center of the underparts is whitish. Females generally resemble males but may be slightly duller and greener on the head. Immatures have a greenish head, grayish upperparts, pale underparts, and reduced blue coloration.
value.rangeHabitat: This tanager occurs from southeastern Mexico through Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, and Panama, continuing into western and northern Colombia and western Ecuador. It is primarily a bird of tropical lowlands and foothills, generally from sea level to about 1,500 meters. Suitable environments include humid forest canopy and borders, clearings, river edges, mature secondary woodland, plantations, and well-vegetated gardens. Its ability to use disturbed and regenerating habitats helps it persist in many human-modified landscapes.
value.migrationStatus: The Golden-hooded Tanager is mainly nonmigratory and remains within its tropical range throughout the year. Local movements may occur in response to fruit availability.
value.breeding: The nest is a small open cup placed in vegetation, commonly in a tree fork, dense foliage, or occasionally among cultivated banana plants. It is built from fine plant fibers and other soft material. The usual clutch contains two whitish eggs marked with brown. Both parents participate in caring for the nestlings. The species may raise more than one brood in a season, and young from an earlier nesting attempt have sometimes been observed helping adults feed chicks from a later brood.
value.dietFeeding: Golden-hooded Tanagers eat small fruits, berries, and insects. Fruit is often swallowed whole, making the bird a likely disperser of seeds within tropical woodland and regenerating vegetation. It searches for food from the middle levels to the canopy, taking fruit from branches and foliage and gleaning insects from leaves and twigs. Birds may also forage along forest edges, in plantations, and in fruiting trees near gardens.
value.behavior: This active tanager is usually encountered in pairs, family parties, or small groups. It also joins mixed-species feeding flocks moving through forest edges and treetops. Foraging birds hop quickly among branches and often remain above eye level, although they descend around low fruiting vegetation. The call is a sharp, thin note, while the song consists of a rapid, rather unmusical series of ticking or rattling sounds. Outside nesting activity, individuals frequently feed close to other fruit-eating birds.

conservation.status: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List.
conservation.populationTrend: Stable; the total global population has not been quantified, but the species remains widespread and is considered fairly common in suitable habitat.
